description: We’re space systems engineering students from Pakistan building PARWAAZ, a game that lets students design, launch, and operate a spacecraft. In our first playable mission, Fire Watch, players build a wildfire-monitoring satellite within limits on mass, power, cost, and time. Before launch, they watch the game recalculate how changes to propellant, tanks, and structure affect one another. When a design exceeds a limit, the game explains what happened and suggests one change to try.
summary:
Parwaaz ("flight" in Urdu) is a bilingual game that teaches how real spacecraft are designed. Players pick a mission, such as a small satellite that spots wildfires from orbit, then choose the instrument, solar array, battery, engine, radio and thermal parts. Live gauges show mass, power, budget, radio link, thermal, schedule and propellant, calculated with standard engineering methods rather than invented game rules. A mission can only launch once every subsystem's numbers agree, which engineers call closing the design. Players then launch, fly years of operations, and receive a debrief that compares their satellite with a real NASA mission.

Space systems engineering is rarely taught outside universities, and almost never in Urdu. Parwaaz runs on the web and on Android in English and Urdu, with a Beginner mode for newcomers and an Engineer mode that shows the underlying numbers and equations, so students can learn by designing, failing and improving.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Parwaaz walks the player through the five stages of a space mission: Briefing, Design, Close the loop, Launch & operate, and Debrief. There are four missions (a wildfire-watching satellite in low Earth orbit, a geostationary communications satellite, a lunar orbiter and a Mars orbiter) plus a free-play Sandbox.

HOW IT WORKS

In the Design Bay the player selects parts for each subsystem. Every choice updates seven budgets: launch mass against launcher capacity, end-of-life solar power, cost, radio link margin, radiator area, schedule and propellant. Closing the design iterates dry mass, propellant, tanks and structure until the launch mass converges, and shows each iteration. The mission then flies through launch, eclipse, first downlink and years of operations, and each event passes, degrades or fails according to the player's margins. The debrief scores science return, cost and robustness, gives an engineering insight, and compares the design with a real NASA mission (MODIS on Terra and Aqua for the wildfire mission). Players can share a result card.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The game makes the trade-offs of spacecraft design visible to students with no engineering background. Everything is available in English and Urdu, with a guide character, Sitara, who explains what is blocking the design. A Sources & data screen lists where every constant and equation comes from.

TOOLS

Built with Flutter and Dart from a single codebase for web and Android. Mission, part and launcher data are stored as JSON. Fonts: Inter, Space Grotesk, Source Code Pro and Noto Nastaliq Urdu.

CREATIVITY

Instead of flying a rocket, the core mechanic is the systems-engineering loop itself: the player wins by making the numbers agree.

USE OF AI

AI tools were used for ideation, coding and debugging. The demo video is a screen recording of the app; its narration is an AI-generated voice, and the video was edited with AI assistance.
